right_thought:
Also rendered right resolve or right intention. The scriptures distinguish two kinds: **mundane right resolve** — the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill-will, and the thought of harmlessness; and **supramundane right resolve** — the undefiled thought corresponding to the four noble truths (*Saṃyukta-āgama*, fascicle 28, sūtra 785; *Majjhima Nikāya* 117, *Mahācattārīsaka Sutta*).

The three address different things:

- **Renunciation** (nekkhamma, the thought of renunciation) — counteracting the thought of desire: letting go of the compulsion that "there must always be something," not merely suppressing desire;
- **Non-ill-will** (avyāpāda, the thought of non-ill-will) — counteracting the thought of ill-will. The treatises define "ill-will" as the mind that **wishes to strike, to bind, to kill**, so what non-ill-will stills is **the mind of harm**, not an emotion, and it is **not equivalent to making no judgement** — to judge a certain view as wrong without giving rise to the intention to harm is still non-ill-will;
- **Harmlessness** (avihiṃsā, the thought of harmlessness) — counteracting the thought of harm. The treatises take "harmlessness" as a wholesome mental factor, **of one substance with compassion**: it is not merely "not wishing to harm," but wishing that others be free from suffering.

The second and third address the same other beings (the treatises group them together under the single heading of counteracting ill-will), yet one level is **the stilling of hostility** and the other is **the wish that others be free from suffering**, so they are not a synonymous repetition.

*Majjhima Nikāya* 19, the *Dvedhāvitakka Sutta*, records that before his awakening the Buddha divided thoughts into two classes: desire, ill-will, and harm as one class, and renunciation, non-ill-will, and harmlessness as the other; when the former arose he knew them to be "harmful to oneself, harmful to others, harmful to both," and the latter the reverse — **the same mental event, turned in a different direction, is either wrong or right** — and so this belongs to the purification of mental action. Right thought stands after [[right_view|right view]]: once the view is established, the orientation of the mind turns accordingly.
right_action: Abstention from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and from sexual misconduct; guarding bodily action. These coincide with the first three of the [[five_precepts|five precepts]]. The treatises judge these three by the standard of **precepts by nature**: **precepts by nature** are those that are evil in themselves and are transgressed without waiting for a rule laid down by the Buddha (whether or not the Buddha has laid down the rule, to transgress them is always an offence); **precepts of prohibition** are those that are not evil in themselves and that the Buddha laid down in order to protect the remaining precepts and to put an end to reproach (such as not drinking alcohol). "Arising with respect to the object of a sentient being" is only a concomitant feature, not the criterion of classification.
right_samadhi: One-pointedness of mind, namely the [[four_dhyanas|four dhyānas and eight concentrations]] and the like; it is the power of concentration on which contemplative wisdom depends. The scriptures stress that right concentration is only called "right" when it arises together with the other seven factors — if there is absorption alone without right view and right mindfulness, it is a mundane concentration that can lead to rebirth in the heavens but does not escape birth and death. The treatises therefore distinguish the two, **the criterion lying in whether they are defiled or undefiled and whether they correspond to undefiled wisdom** (*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 28): mundane concentration is defiled and does not take the four noble truths as its object; supramundane concentration corresponds to undefiled wisdom and takes the four noble truths as its object.
nonself_seal:
All dharmas — whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether the world of sentient beings or the material world — lack an independent, unchanging, self-existent nature. "Self" (ātman) has a determinate meaning in the Indian context: only that which possesses all four senses — permanent (unchanging), one (independent), master (self-existent) and sovereign (controlling) — is called a "self." The Buddhist [[anatta|non-self]] denies that any one of these four senses exists in any dharma.

Non-self is therefore not the nihilistic assertion "I do not exist" but "no dharma possesses the substantially real character of being permanent, one and sovereign." This formulation is continuous with [[emptiness|emptiness]], but it must be noted that **"emptiness" here does not mean "nothing"**: according to the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, "Examination of the Four Noble Truths," emptiness is "the absence of own-nature" (because of dependent origination there is no independent, unchanging entity), and it does not deny the functioning of dharmas through dependent origination. Thus "emptiness is non-self" is a mutual statement of the meaning of the absence of own-nature, not a nihilism.
